planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in fall or early spring in fast-draining, gritty soil; established plants resent summer irrigation once dormant after bloom.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to very light shade, ideally on a slope or in a rock garden setting; showy phlox is native to dry pine and oak woodlands of the Pacific Northwest and interior West, where it blooms in loose, open clusters of pink to lavender notched-petal flowers in late spring. The woody-based clumps go summer-dormant in the wild and should be kept on the dry side after flowering to mimic natural conditions and prevent crown rot. It resents heavy clay and winter wet far more than cold, so raised beds or scree plantings suit it best. Avoid mulching close to the woody crown.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Direct sow in fall so seed overwinters in place; natural cold-moist stratification breaks dormancy and seedlings emerge with spring moisture.

directions: Grow in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, mimicking the sagebrush steppe and dry montane slopes where longleaf phlox occurs across much of the interior West. Slender stems carry narrow, grass-like leaves and clusters of fragrant pink, white, or lavender flowers from mid to late spring, making a fine low-water addition to xeric borders and native wildflower plantings. Plants rely on excellent drainage and go dormant in summer heat, so withhold supplemental water once bloom finishes. It self-sows readily where conditions suit it but is not aggressive in garden settings.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Set out transplants after last frost in lean, rocky or sandy, very well-drained soil; established plants tolerate extreme heat and drought.

directions: Plant in full sun and gravelly, alkaline, fast-draining soil, as found on the limestone caprock and rocky prairies of the southern Great Plains and Texas Panhandle where this skullcap is native. Compact, gray-green mounded foliage is studded with small violet-blue, two-lipped flowers from late spring through fall, with the heaviest flush after rain. It is exceptionally drought- and heat-tolerant once established and makes a durable edging or rock-garden plant that needs no supplemental fertilizer. Avoid rich, moisture-retentive soils, which shorten its lifespan and encourage rot.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil; deadhead spent stems to encourage repeat bloom through summer.

directions: Grow in full sun to light shade in average, well-drained garden soil; Persian cornflower, native to the Caucasus, produces deeply cut, silvery-green foliage and large, fringed rose-pink to lavender-pink flowerheads with pale centers from early to midsummer. Cutting plants back hard after the first flush of bloom often triggers a second round of flowers into fall and keeps the somewhat floppy stems tidier. It spreads steadily by rhizomes and benefits from division every three to four years to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding. The cut flowers hold up well in arrangements.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into prepared meadow soil, or start indoors and transplant; tolerates poor, compacted, or chalky soils that few other meadow perennials will take.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean to average, well-drained soil, including poor or chalky ground where lusher meadow plants struggle. Black knapweed produces wiry, branched stems topped with thistle-like, dark bristly bracts and reddish-purple tufted flowers from midsummer into fall, making it an outstanding long-season nectar source for bumblebees, butterflies, and skippers. It is a mainstay of European wildflower meadow mixes and naturalizes readily by seed, so site it where some spread is welcome rather than in tightly managed borders. Mow or cut back meadow plantings once in late fall to reduce excess self-seeding.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in gritty, sharply drained soil; good drainage over winter is more important than soil fertility.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, gritty, well-drained soil, as befits this low mat-forming knapweed native to rocky slopes of the Caucasus. Finely divided, silvery-gray foliage spreads into a tight carpet studded with soft pink thistle-like flowerheads from late spring into summer, making it a durable choice for rock gardens, dry walls, and sunny edging where taller perennials would overwhelm it. It spreads by creeping rhizomes to form a slowly expanding patch and tolerates drought and poor soil far better than excess winter moisture. Shear lightly after the main flush of bloom to tidy the foliage and encourage sporadic rebloom.
